title: Foundations: Why a Custom Agent's Economics Are Different
tierLabel: No infrastructure — just the mental model
summary: When you build the agent loop yourself, every cost lever that Claude Code's harness handled for you becomes something you must design and own explicitly.
whyItMatters: Misunderstanding this is the single biggest source of runaway cost in custom agents: teams port an interactive, human-supervised mental model onto an unattended, high-volume system.

concepts.heading: Five things a harness gives you for free
concepts.body: Claude Code (or any polished agentic CLI) quietly handles: context compaction (/compact), model selection (/model), a human watching for runaway loops, prompt structuring for cache hits, and usage visibility (/usage). Building your own agent means each of these becomes a design decision, not a given.

concepts.heading: Volume changes the math
concepts.body: An interactive developer session is bounded by how long a person sits at a keyboard — tens of turns a day. A production agent can run thousands of unattended invocations. Per-call cost multiplied by volume dominates; a $0.002 inefficiency per call is irrelevant at 50 calls/day and existential at 500,000.

concepts.heading: The four things you now own
concepts.body: 1) Context growth — nothing stops it unless you write the stopping logic. 2) Tool schema tax — every registered tool costs input tokens on every single call, whether used or not. 3) Runaway loops — no human is present to notice and hit Escape. 4) Cost visibility — you must instrument it yourself, off raw API responses or provider billing metrics.

concepts.heading: Why this workshop uses Strands, not raw API calls
concepts.body: The exercises below build agents with the Strands Agents SDK (AWS's open-source agent framework) running on Amazon Bedrock, rather than hand-rolled loops around a raw messages.create call. Strands already ships a real agent loop, a conversation manager, a hooks system, and native Bedrock prompt/tool caching -- the exact primitives this workshop is teaching you to reason about. Where Strands has a built-in for a pattern, the exercise uses it directly instead of reinventing it.

exercises.title: Measure the fixed cost of your own tool schemas
exercises.goal: See, in real tokens, what you are paying on every single call before the model does any work.
steps: Install the SDK: `pip install strands-agents strands-agents-tools`.
Build a minimal Strands agent with 3-5 tools (reuse your real tools, or the calculator/current_time tools shipped in strands-agents-tools).

Enable native Bedrock token counting on the model and inspect the accumulated usage after a single call. → Expect: a non-zero input token count that includes your tool schemas even on a trivial request.
Multiply that per-call fixed cost by your expected daily call volume. → Expect: a number that makes the 'tool tax' concrete rather than abstract.

code.content:
from strands import Agent, tool
from strands.models import BedrockModel

@tool
def search_orders(order_id: str = "", status: str = "") -> str:
    """Search customer orders by id, date range, or status."""
    return f"Searched orders with order_id={order_id!r} status={status!r}"

# add the rest of your real tools here

model = BedrockModel(
    model_id="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5",
    use_native_token_count=True,
)

agent = Agent(model=model, tools=[search_orders])

response = agent("placeholder")

input_tokens = response.metrics.accumulated_usage.get("inputTokens", 0)
print(f"Fixed per-call tool tax (this call's total input tokens): {input_tokens}")

exercises.costImpact: This number is paid on every call regardless of whether any tool is used. At scale it is often the single largest fixed cost in a custom agent, which is why Tab 5 (tool design) and Tab 7 (gateway patterns) exist.
